content: Loa loa is a parasitic filarial nematode, commonly referred to as the eye worm, that causes a condition known as Loa loa filariasis. This parasitic infection is primarily found in regions of Africa and India. Loa loa is one of three filarial nematodes that cause subcutaneous filariasis in humans, the other two being Mansonella streptocerca and Onchocerca volvulus (the latter being responsible for river blindness). The maturing larvae and adult worms of Loa loa inhabit the subcutaneous tissue and fat layers of the human skin, where they induce disease. The immature larvae of Loa loa develop within horseflies of the genus Chrysops (commonly known as deer flies or yellow flies), particularly the species Chrysops dimidiata and Chrysops silacea. These flies transmit the infection to humans through their bites. Morphology Loa loa worms have a simple body structure consisting of a head, body, and tail. Male worms measure between 20 mm and 34 mm in length and 350 μm to 430 μm in width. Female worms are larger, ranging from 20 mm to 70 mm in length and approximately 425 μm in width. Life Cycle The transmission of Loa loa filariasis involves flies from the genus Chrysops, specifically C. silacea and C. dimidiata. During a blood meal, an infected fly introduces third-stage filarial larvae onto the skin of a human host. These larvae penetrate the bite wound and migrate into the subcutaneous tissue, where they mature into adult worms. The adult worms reside in the subcutaneous tissue and produce microfilariae, which are sheathed and exhibit diurnal periodicity. These microfilariae measure 250 to 300 μm in length and 6 to 8 μm in width. Microfilariae can be found in various bodily fluids, including spinal fluid, urine, and sputum. During the day, they are predominantly present in peripheral blood, while during the non-circulating phase, they localize in the lungs. When a fly takes a blood meal from an infected human, it ingests the microfilariae. Inside the fly, the microfilariae shed their sheaths and migrate from the midgut through the hemocoel to the thoracic muscles. Within the thoracic muscles, the microfilariae develop into first-stage larvae and subsequently into third-stage infective larvae. These third-stage larvae then migrate to the fly's proboscis, enabling the fly to infect another human during its next blood meal.
